status: Draft from the mishnah and R. Kulp's commentary only (each item carries its mishnah number). To be deepened with Kehati. Definitions are provisional until AnyDaf's master glossary covers them.

principles.t: An animal accounted harmless (tam) that does damage: its owner pays half damages, and the payment cannot exceed the value of the animal itself.

When it is unclear whether a loss was caused by the goring, the money in doubt is split: the owner pays half of the half he might owe, a quarter damages. The Mishnah here follows Sumchus (money in doubt is split), not the rule of 3:11 that the claimant must bring proof. The halakha follows the Sages: nothing is paid unless the claimant proves it (Kehati).

Someone who brings his belongings into another person's property without permission is liable if they cause damage there, and gets nothing if they are damaged there. The householder can say: I never gave you permission (trespassing).

With permission the laws reverse: if the visitor's belongings are damaged, the owner of the property is liable. (It is not stated, but can be assumed, that the visitor is then not liable for damage his belongings cause.)
A person who causes a miscarriage pays for the offspring, to the husband (or his heirs). An ox's owner does not, because Exodus 21:22 speaks of men fighting.
principles.note: R. Kulp cautions that this exemption is not a blanket statement about abortion.

principles.t: The pit is the second of the four archetypal causes of damage. Whoever digs or uncovers a pit, in a private or public domain, is liable if an animal falls in and dies. The same holds for any hole (trench, cavern, ditch, channel).
A hole counts as a pit if it is ten handbreadths (about a yard) deep, the depth normal for causing an animal's death. Shallower: no liability for a death, but liability for an injury.
If a pit has two owners, the last one to leave it uncovered is liable. If it was properly covered and an animal still fell in, he is not liable.

Pit liability is limited to the animal itself: not the load or trappings, and not a person who falls in, even a child or a slave. This is learned from Exodus 21:33, 'an ox, and not a person; an ass, and not trappings'.

'Ox' in the Torah is an example. For eight laws, including falling into a pit, the rule applies to every animal, wild animals and birds too. The Torah says ox because oxen were the most commonly used animals.

terms.def: An animal 'accounted harmless'. If it gores, its owner pays half damages, up to the animal's own value.
Half damages is the payment for harm done by a tam. A quarter damages is half of half damages: the share the mishnah awards when half of the half is in doubt.
Entering another person's property without his permission (trespassing). In 5:2-5:3 this decides who is liable.
The payment an ox's owner makes to the family when his ox kills a person (Exodus 21:30). In 5:3 it also applies when the ox kills someone by falling into a cistern.
One of the four archetypal causes of damage listed in the first mishnah of the tractate. The pit (bor) is the second.
Exodus 21:33-34: one who opens or digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or donkey falls in, pays the owner of the animal and keeps the carcass.
A measure of length. Ten handbreadths, about a yard, is the depth of a pit that can cause death.

debates.title: Does permission to enter mean the owner is watching the visitor's things?
debates.a: The anonymous view: by letting him in, the householder implicitly accepts responsibility for his belongings, so he is liable if they are damaged.
debates.b: Rabbi (Rabbi Judah Hanasi): letting someone in is not accepting responsibility; the householder is liable only if he explicitly agreed to watch over them. Otherwise the visitor is still responsible for his own things.

debates.title: How is the offspring valued?
debates.a: The first view: assess the woman's value before the pregnancy and after; the difference is the payment.
debates.b: Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel: a pregnant woman is worth less, since childbirth was dangerous, so that method cannot work. Instead assess what the offspring itself would have been worth.

debates.title: Mishnah against mishnah: who has to prove it?
debates.a: 3:8 (as Kulp describes it): the burden of proof is on the claimant, so with no proof he gets nothing.
debates.b: 5:1: where it is unclear, the two sides split the money. Kulp: this shows the Mishnah is not a law book without contradictions but a collection of laws and traditions from which a capable judge could decide.
